assembly_scope: Nine exact revisions have paired admissible assessments. The nine retained initial revisions await corrected bindings or replacement revisions.

assessments.reasoning: RFC 4180 Status and Abstract call this an informational common format. Sections 1–3, especially §2 rules 1–7 and the ABNF, establish CRLF records, optional matching-form header, commas, and quoted/escaped fields. Section 3 acknowledges deployed variation. The sample is LF-delimited and does not establish exact RFC 4180 conformance.

RFC 7111 Abstract and §1.1 identify the underlying RFC 4180 media type. Its selector grammar and processing in §§3–4 operate on existing rows, columns and cells, and §5.1 updates the media registration. This is a scope boundary, with RFC 4180 supplying the record representation.

challenge.method: Checked RFC 4180 against the LF-only origin and W3C CSVW annotated-table model.
challenge.results: RFC 4180 is an informational common format and its line convention is CRLF. CSVW supplies separate tabular metadata and mapping; the plain source rows remain record representation.

limitations: Informational description of a common format. It explicitly acknowledges implementation variation. The native sample's LF line ends are outside its CRLF record convention.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.

assessments.reasoning: The exact RFC supports the proposition in its Abstract and §§2–4, including URI examples in §2 and range processing in §4.2. The frozen locator names §3 Fragment Identification Methods and §4 Processing of Fragment Identifiers. Actual labels are §2 Fragment Identification Methods, §3 Fragment Identification Syntax and §4 Fragment Identifier Processing. The operative examples and affected precise citation require correction before promotion.

challenge.method: Tested row, col and cell selectors, wildcard and out-of-bounds handling against RFC 7111 §§2–4 and media registration §5.1.
challenge.results: Range selection is real, but the selector appears in the URI fragment and works on an existing entity. The frozen pinpoint mislabels the controlling section, so withhold this revision pending repair.

limitations: The fragment occurs in the URI and has its own syntax. This evidence concerns CSV-content scope and leaves any independent selector identity question open.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.
Blocking frozen bindings: support-csv-fragment-uri-scope.

assessments.reasoning: RFC 8259 Abstract and §1 define lightweight data interchange and distinguish four primitive types and two structured types. §2 allows any serialized JSON value at the top level. §§4–5 define the object member and array element structures. The adopted descriptive use matches the text and December 2017 edition.

The newly retrieved GameMaker LTS manual describes .yy resource metadata as JSON-like and names GameMaker-managed asset information. This is context for the application vocabulary only. The HTTP response digests differ from frozen source revision 1, including after multiple ordinary header profiles. There is no exact fresh receipt for this binding.

4D version 19 Project folder and applicationName.4DProject identify a development file used to designate and launch the project. This gives application context for the pinned sample, whose bytes independently parse as a JSON object. The 4D section does not prescribe JSON grammar, or prove all such project files use this exact representation.

The endpoint now redirects to extensionless June 16, 2022 Core draft HTML. Sections 1 and 4.3 show JSON documents used as schemas, with keyword semantics supplied by the separate vocabulary in §4.3.1. The frozen citation conflates §4.3 JSON Schema Documents with §4.3.1 JSON Schema Objects and Keywords. All observed response digests differ from the frozen revision; this contextual binding needs a new exact source decision and citation.

challenge.method: Tested JSON object/array and top-level primitives, application-specific keys, JSON Schema constraints and the RFC 9535 JSONPath usage.
challenge.results: RFC 8259 governs serialized values. GameMaker and 4D supply host conventions; JSON Schema and JSONPath have separate constraint/query semantics. Two bound context snapshots lack exact receipts, with an additional JSON Schema section-title error. Withhold frozen revision.

limitations: This lead concerns RFC 8259 JSON. Project-specific metadata names, query syntax, schema vocabularies and API/runtime interpretation stay in their respective scopes.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.
Blocking frozen bindings: context-json-rfc8259-serialized-values-1, context-json-rfc8259-serialized-values-3.

assessments.reasoning: The official March 2018 1.0.0 title, Abstract, and §§1–1.1 describe a JSON-derived interchange format intended for human authors, adopting limited ES5.1 productions. §§2–7 and 9.2 delimit the values and extensions. §§10–11 distinguish a parser accepting the format from a generator producing it. Source comments and property names are grammar rather than executable host commands.

RFC 8259 §§2–7 independently bound baseline JSON value grammar and string/number rules. Single quotes, unquoted keys, comments, hexadecimal and trailing commas belong to the JSON5 source scope. Comparing the document models does not transfer permissions or execution semantics.

challenge.method: Compared 1.0.0 syntax and two pinned examples against RFC 8259 and the alternative that ECMAScript features or package scripts make the format executable.
challenge.results: The borrowed productions extend lexical and value syntax. The package scripts are data properties whose behavior requires a host. Comments and human-editability do not establish a schema or expression model.

limitations: The ECMAScript productions picked up by JSON5 are scoped lexical and syntactic features. Host package loading and command interpretation do not follow from the data grammar.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.

assessments.reasoning: At October2021, official README Overview and Getting Started call GraphQL a query language and name the type system, execution semantics, static validation and introspection. The Type System example demonstrates schema declarations. The README is descriptive even though it calls the specification a Working Draft. The normative findings use the published edition instead.

The October 2021 Introduction, §§2.2–2.3 and §3 distinguish executable operation documents and type-system forms. §§7.2–7.2.1 allow different response encodings and describe JSON as common. Treating GraphQL as JSON or HTTP alone would omit its query and type-system rules.

challenge.method: Compared official Type System and executable document sections with the pinned schema and operations samples, then challenged the HTTP, JSON and runtime alternatives.
challenge.results: The language has separately governed declarations, static validation and operation semantics. Response serialization is a separate optional choice. The pinned mixed sample is not evidence of full conformance.

limitations: The language identity includes document and type-system forms in the October 2021 specification. Execution engines, transports, and response serializations retain their own scopes.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.

assessments.reasoning: The official proto2 guide opens with the .proto language and generation of data access classes. Defining A Message Type establishes the schema declarations. JSON Mapping explicitly concerns encoding and Options concern how declarations are handled. The subject is the source schema language scoped by this evidence to proto2 documentation.

The official binary encoding guide Message Structure distinguishes field numbers, wire types and payloads from names and declared types supplied by the .proto definition at decoding. It identifies the alternative category as wire format, without adding schema-language norms.

The official proto2 syntax reference announces incomplete lexical detail and calls C++ protoc definitive. Syntax documents the proto2 source statement, providing version context. This does not replace the scoped guide or support a claim of complete proto2 conformance.

The official proto3 page identifies its edition and incomplete parser description, its explicit proto3 syntax statement, and its own normal field form. A similar source extension does not import proto3 field rules into a proto2 claim.

challenge.method: Compared the .proto address-book program text with official binary encoding, JSON mapping, proto3 and generated APIs.
challenge.results: The declared field names, types, cardinality and nested declarations form the governed Protobuf schema language. Serializing messages, running protoc and choosing generated accessors are separate.

limitations: The proposed entity concerns the schema declaration notation. Proto2 is the source scope for this cohort. Generated APIs, runtime tools, message encodings and text-format values remain separate.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.

assessments.reasoning: The proto2 Syntax prose states that omitting syntax selects proto2 and recommends making the choice explicit. The claim correctly attributes that documented rule and conditions it on absence of both a syntax declaration and an Editions declaration. No version-specific protoc behavior was inferred.

The official proto3 Syntax production selects proto3 via an explicit syntax statement. This supplies the edition alternative, not independent corroboration for the legacy default. A Protobuf Editions declaration is outside the frozen condition.

challenge.method: Compared the pinned sample with no declaration to proto2 Syntax, explicit proto3 Syntax and the Editions guide.
challenge.results: Proto2 reference documents the legacy default for an undeclared file. An explicit edition or proto3 syntax is outside the condition. This is documentation review without claiming an execution on a specific compiler build.

limitations: This documents the legacy implicit form for a source without a syntax or a Protobuf Editions declaration. It does not reproduce a version-specific compiler result or validate the entire fixture.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.

assessments.reasoning: The proto2 guide Specifying Field Cardinality assigns singular required and optional forms and says repeated fields support zero or more ordered values. Required is discouraged but still documented. Map entries and low-level wire occurrences are distinct questions.

The proto3 Normal Field production permits repeated and optional modifiers without a required label. This scopes a contrasting edition, and the same named language family does not make that production govern the proto2 candidate.

challenge.method: Compared the three sample labels and tested the counterexamples of omitted required fields, zero repeated entries and proto3’s changed syntax against the guides.
challenge.results: The proto2 guide supports the exact labels and repeated order, while also discouraging required fields and keeping map and wire multiplicity distinct.

limitations: The guide discourages required fields and explicitly notes their removal from proto3 and Editions. Maps and oneof declarations follow separate rules.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.

assessments.reasoning: The official Overview states a human-authored configuration format mapped unambiguously to a hash table and gives named owner/database tables. The index inclusion follows the source-governed declaration model for tables, dotted paths and arrays of tables. The claim correctly states the overview description and does not derive application execution from it.

TOML v1.0.0 Objectives describes the hash-table projection. Table and Array of Tables identify path declarations, duplicate rejection and current-array-element binding. MIME Type also expressly classifies the transport representation as application/toml. Both attributes can coexist within the index declaration criterion.

Cargo 1.85.0 Manifest Format and The edition field locate [package] edition as Cargo policy affecting Rust compilation. TOML handles table/key/value interpretation, while Cargo owns the field and convention. This checked edition context is intentionally outside the core TOML claim scope.

The exact RustSec example documents application choices under advisories, database, output, target and yanked. Its bytes also equal the pinned Linguist example. The audit setting meanings come from RustSec, while table and value syntax belongs to TOML. The two files are duplicate content here and do not supply independent corroboration.

challenge.method: Challenged inclusion by TOML’s format label, MIME type, and hash-table result, then checked source-governed table declarations and Cargo/RustSec host-specific meaning.
challenge.results: TOML is a file format and a declarative configuration notation under the actual Index criterion. Dotted path definitions, table declarations, and current array-element binding are document rules. Host package and audit policy is not part of its core declaration model.

limitations: The proposed language identity rests on the separately evidenced native v1.0.0 declaration semantics. Configuration interchange is an overlapping use. Application-specific keys and actions are outside the language identity.
The assessment is confined to the named documents and revision scope.
